So let's begin with some background on how the development bond came to be.
Many Canadian municipalities accept only letters of credit or LCs as security against development agreements.
The drawback of LCs is that banks require them to be cash collateralized.
This means land developers not only have to fund the construction work, but they also have to post cash to the bank to secure the LC.
The use of LCs ties up developers cash flow and increases their costs which down the line translates to more cost to their customers, the home purchasers.

Today we are here to talk about an alternative instrument to LCs, which is the modern pay on demand bond, which provides municipalities with the same level of financial protection that LCs provide, while not infringing upon the developers cash flow and liquidity.
This bond form is a pay on demand credit instrument that mirrors the key features that LCs offer.
Next slide please.
So the intent is for the development bond to be an additional tool in the toolbox of options alongside letters of credit that the city of Saskatoon will offer to their development community.
This bond provides financial assurance to a municipality that a developer will successfully complete all obligations under the development agreement.
This bond may be reduced upon achievement of certain construction milestones and ultimately released upon achievement of final acceptance certificate, much the same as LCs would operate.
Next slide please.
Thank you.
And so let us turn to the technical aspects of the bond wording itself.
Most importantly, the bond is a pay on demand instrument, meaning that there is no oneness on the municipality to prove that the developer is in default of the development agreement.
It is written into the bond language that the municipality has sold and absolute discretion to declare a developer in default and to file a demand for funds.
Once the surety receives the municipality's demand for funds, they must pay.
It is written into the bond language that the surety has no right to defend against the municipality's demand.
Once the surety receives the municipality's demand, they have a defined payment period of seven days to provide payment to the municipality.
I should note here that some municipalities have opted for 10 days in their bond wording, so there is an option.
The bond is also irrevocable in that no amendments are permissible without expressed written request from all parties involved.
The bond is evergreen in that it automatically renews per annum.
The bond also includes a notice of cancellation provision, meaning that should the surety wish to cancel the bond, they must provide the municipality with written notice of their intent.
The developer must then provide the municipality with replacement security, either in the form of a new bond from a different surety or an LC from the bank within the stated notice period.
Partial drawdowns are permitted.
The bond amount may be reduced but only with expressed written approval from the municipality.
Next slide please.
This slide is a visual representation of the previous slide just to demonstrate that the development bonds satisfies all the same key features that LC's do.
Moving along to the next slide.
Here we will speak to the creditworthiness of surety companies.
Surety's are regulated by the office of the superintendent of financial institutions or Osphe for short, who is also the regulating body that governs banks.
Osphe regularly reviews each surety's capitalization to ensure that they are adequately capitalized to be able to pay out on any bond claims that arise.
We also recommend that municipalities accept bonds from the top tier of surety companies who have an external credit rating of a minus or better, which is synonymous with excellence.

Surety's will perform a thorough review of the developers financial statements and credit quality.
They will also want to know that the developer has a strong track record of successfully completing development agreements in the past.
Finally, they will also review project specific details regarding project economic such as the budget construction schedule and selection of construction trades.
Surety companies obtain the developers corporate guarantee to secure the bond.
They do not take cash collateral to secure the bond the way that bond banks take cash to secure LCs.
